items.title: Arrival
items.pace: Land, get IC cards sorted, no fixed plans beyond dinner.
items.tldr: Land, sort out IC cards, and ease into Tokyo with a no-reservation conveyor-sushi dinner.
items.body:
Get an IC card per person on arrival (Suica, PASMO, or a Tourist PASMO at either airport) — everything else in this guide assumes you have one. Settle in, then keep dinner easy: Uobei Genki Sushi in Shibuya needs no reservation and moves fast even for a group of six.

It is counter seating and cash only, so make sure everyone has yen before you leave the airport.

items.title: Tsukiji, then the anchor dinner
items.pace: An early market breakfast, a deliberately light afternoon, then the trip's one serious dinner.
items.tldr: A dawn graze through Tsukiji Outer Market, an unstructured afternoon, then RyuGin — the trip's one splurge dinner.
items.body:
Start at Tsukiji Outer Market between 6:30 and 9 AM. Saturday is a full trading day on the wholesale-market calendar its shops follow, and the lanes are calm before the 10 AM–1 PM peak.

Graze stall to stall in pairs or trios rather than moving as one block of six — the market's own site asks visitors not to move through the narrow lanes in large groups.

Then let the afternoon stay unstructured. Tsukiji, Ginza and Hibiya sit within about 2 km of each other, so you can drift west on foot instead of planning a crossing.

Dinner is Nihonryori RyuGin in Hibiya (see Food & shopping) — book through your hotel concierge as soon as accommodation is confirmed, since October dates open on Sept 1, 2026. ⚠ RyuGin will not accept a reservation from anyone who declares a food allergy, and cannot serve guests who don't eat fish or seafood. Settle that across all six before the concierge calls.
constraints: RyuGin reservation required — book via hotel concierge, see Food & shopping
RyuGin: no reservations from guests declaring food allergies; everyone must eat fish/seafood; ages 10+ only

items.title: Asakusa, Harajuku, Shinjuku
items.pace: A temple-and-food-street morning, a shrine and a garden in the afternoon, dinner in Omoide Yokocho.
items.tldr: Senso-ji and the Nakamise food street in the morning, Meiji Jingu and Shinjuku Gyoen in the afternoon, dinner at a group-friendly Omoide Yokocho izakaya.
items.body:
Senso-ji and Nakamise-dori make an easy, food-forward morning — snack your way down the approach street rather than committing to a sit-down lunch. The main hall opens at 6:30 AM through October, so an early start is there if jet lag has you up.

Both afternoon stops shut early. Meiji Jingu's gates close at 4:40 PM in October, and Shinjuku Gyoen stops admitting at 4:00 PM. Do the shrine first, then the garden, and treat 4 PM as the hard edge of the day.

Neither market is a Sunday option — Toyosu is closed, and roughly half of Tsukiji's outer-market shops follow the same calendar. Saturday already covers Tsukiji.

Dinner is Torien in Omoide Yokocho — a 150-seat izakaya rather than the small counters most of the alley runs on, so six of you eat together.

items.title: Toyosu and teamLab
items.pace: A bay-area morning, gallery midday, wagyu dinner back in Ginza.
items.tldr: Toyosu Market and teamLab Planets by day, a self-booked wagyu yakiniku dinner in Ginza at night.
items.body:
Toyosu Market is open today — browse rather than queue for Sushi Dai/Daiwa Sushi's counters (2–5 hour waits, and a party of six will likely be split in two). teamLab Planets is a few minutes away and fills the rest of the morning and early afternoon.

Shinjuku Gyoen is closed on Mondays, so it isn't on today's plan — Sunday already covers it.

Dinner is Yakiniku Ushigoro in Ginza, a short ride back from Toyosu, booked online rather than through a concierge. It is the trip's second-most expensive meal, not a casual night — courses run ¥16,000–32,000 before the 10% service charge.

plan_b.body: teamLab Planets sells timed-entry tickets and closes for maintenance on irregular dates. If Oct 19 turns out to be one, Tokyo Tower's Main Deck is the drop-in substitute — open 9:00 AM–11:00 PM (last entry 10:30 PM), ¥1,200–1,500 adult depending on whether you book online or buy at the window, and roughly 15 minutes from the Ginza dinner.

items.title: Yanaka and Ameyoko, then departure
items.pace: A relaxed morning food crawl, then the airport.
items.tldr: One last grazing morning through Yanaka Ginza and Ameyoko before heading to the airport.
items.body:
Yanaka Ginza (via Nippori Station) and Ameya-Yokocho (Ueno–Okachimachi) are a short hop apart and both work as pure grazing — no sit-down meal to plan around a flight. Ameyoko is calmest on a weekday morning, which this is.

Work backward from your flight using the airport transit times in the Transit tab — Haneda is faster to reach from central Tokyo than Narita if your return flight gives you the choice.

title: Health & pharmacy
body:
Emergency numbers: police 110, ambulance/fire 119 — both free, 24/7, no area code needed. A non-emergency medical triage line, #7119, exists for uncertain cases; expect a wait for English-language support on any of these.

Pharmacies (drugstores) are widespread, but Japanese pharmacies can't fill a foreign prescription — bring enough of any regular medication for the trip. Some common US over-the-counter cold and allergy medicines (anything with pseudoephedrine, e.g. Sudafed, NyQuil, Advil Cold & Sinus) are restricted or banned in Japan; check Japan Customs' import rules before packing if anyone in the group takes one.

⚠ The current US State Department travel advisory level for Japan could not be verified against a primary source — travel.state.gov blocks automated access. Check travel.state.gov directly before departure.

title: Etiquette & language
body:
Japan is a no-tipping culture — leaving cash on the table causes confusion, and staff have been known to chase guests down to return it. Service is already priced in.

At izakaya, an unrequested small starter (otoshi, a few hundred yen per person) lands on the table automatically and appears on the bill — it isn't a scam or an optional order. Calling "sumimasen" to get a server's attention is normal; nobody comes to the table unprompted the way US service does.

Chopstick basics: never stick them upright in a rice bowl, never pass food chopstick-to-chopstick, and use the opposite end (or provided serving chopsticks) when taking from a shared plate. Shoes come off before stepping onto tatami seating, common at traditional and izakaya spots.

Situational phrases for the trip — allergy/dietary, reservations, ordering — are on the Trip Kit tab.
